\chapter{Eating Out}
\label{ch:ml-eating-out}
\hlchaptermodality{92}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name food, find a place that serves it, and ask for the bill.}

From cold: the general word for food, the eating place, the bill, and the rule that a borrowed word keeps only the meaning its borrowers needed.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bhakṣaṇaṁ]{\ml{ഭക്ഷണം} (bhakṣaṇaṁ) — food}

\label{lesson:ML-C92-bhakshanam}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for a meal. Say the word for cooked rice. Then try to say \textbf{food} and notice that you cannot.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{ഭക്ഷണം}}
\textbf{\ml{ഭക്ഷണം}} — \emph{bhakṣaṇaṁ} — food.

This book has been unusually specific about eating. You own \textbf{\ml{ഊണ്}}, a meal; \textbf{\ml{ചോറ്}}, cooked rice; \textbf{\ml{അരി}}, the raw grain — and until now \textbf{no word for the category all of them belong to.}

That is a common shape in a vocabulary that grows from the particular outward, and it is worth naming when it happens: \textbf{a language course can leave you able to order lunch and unable to say the word \emph{food}.}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{അരി}} & raw rice \\
\textbf{\ml{ചോറ്}} & cooked rice \\
\textbf{\ml{ഊണ്}} & a meal \\
\textbf{\ml{ഭക്ഷണം}} & \textbf{food} — all of it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

It ends in \textbf{\ml{ം}}, so you already know what a \textbf{case ending} will do to it — the \textbf{\ml{ം}} gives way to \textbf{-\ml{ത്ത}-}, as it did on \textbf{\ml{കേരളം}} and \textbf{\ml{പുസ്തകം}}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bhakṣaṇaṁ}
  \item the four food words from narrowest to widest
  \item the verb \emph{to eat}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{bhakṣaṇaṁ}? (\textbf{Food}.) Is it a particular dish or the whole category? (\textbf{The whole category}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hōṭṭal]{\ml{ഹോട്ടൽ} (hōṭṭal) — an eating place}

\label{lesson:ML-C92-hottal}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for food. Say the word for a shop.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{ഹോട്ടൽ}}
\textbf{\ml{ഹോട്ടൽ}} — \emph{hōṭṭal} — a place that serves food.

Read it aloud and you will hear an English word inside it. \textbf{Do not trust it.}

In Kerala a \textbf{\ml{ഹോട്ടൽ}} is ordinarily \textbf{somewhere you go to eat} — a tea-and-meals place, the sort with a board outside listing what is on today. \textbf{A bed is not what the word promises.}

\textbf{\ml{ഹോട്ടലിൽ}} — \emph{hōṭṭalil} — at the eating place. The in-ending attaches the ordinary way.

\begin{culture}
\textbf{A word that crosses into another language stops belonging to the one it came from.} It keeps whichever part of its meaning the borrowers needed and lets the rest go, and afterwards nobody has to consult the original.

That is worth holding on to as a habit, because \textbf{this will not be the last borrowed word you meet here}, and the one thing you must not do is assume it still means what it means at home.

You have already met borrowings that behaved themselves — \textbf{\ml{കാപ്പി}} is coffee and \textbf{\ml{മേശ}} came from Portuguese. \textbf{\ml{ഹോട്ടൽ}} is the first one in this book that would mislead you if you trusted the source.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hōṭṭal}
  \item what you would expect to find there
  \item \emph{hōṭṭalil}
  \item what the English word would have led you to expect instead
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a \emph{hōṭṭal} in Kerala? (\textbf{A place to eat}.) Should a borrowed word be trusted to keep its old meaning? (\textbf{No.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bil]{\ml{ബിൽ} (bil) — the bill}

\label{lesson:ML-C92-bill}



\begin{quote}
Ask how many rupees something is. Then say where you are.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{ബിൽ}}
\textbf{\ml{ബിൽ}} — \emph{bil} — the bill.

Another borrowing, and this one \textbf{kept its meaning intact} — which is the point of meeting it right after one that did not. \textbf{Borrowed words are not all alike; you have to check each one.}

The asking costs nothing new. \textbf{\ml{എത്ര}} has been yours since the distance chapter, and \textbf{\ml{വില}} since the shopping chapter:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{രൂപ}?} & how many rupees? \\
\textbf{\ml{ബിൽ}} & the bill \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The far end of a meal.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bil}
  \item \emph{ethra rūpa?}
  \item which of this chapter's two borrowings changed meaning on the way in
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{bil}? (\textbf{The bill}.) And what is \emph{vila}? (\textbf{Price}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[puṟattŭ kaḻikkal enna ōrmma]{(eating out) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R92-eating-out-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{food}, then say the place that serves it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange — the shape of a meal out}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഹോട്ടലിൽ}} — at the eating place.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഭക്ഷണം}} — food.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ബിൽ}. \ml{എത്ര} \ml{രൂപ}?} — the bill. How many rupees?
\end{quote}

Three new words, and the question at the end is one you have had since the shopping chapter.

\begin{culture}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{came from English} & \textbf{means here} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഹോട്ടൽ}} & \emph{hotel} & \textbf{a place to eat} \\
\textbf{\ml{ബിൽ}} & \emph{bill} & the bill \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{One changed and one did not}, and that is the whole reason they sit in the same chapter. \textbf{A word that crosses into another language stops belonging to the one it came from} — it keeps whichever part of its meaning the borrowers needed and lets the rest go.

So the habit is: \textbf{check each borrowing, do not trust the family.} Recognising the English inside a word tells you how to pronounce it and \textbf{nothing reliable about what it means.}

The food words, meanwhile, finally have a roof. \textbf{\ml{അരി}}, \textbf{\ml{ചോറ്}}, \textbf{\ml{ഊണ്}} were all particular; \textbf{\ml{ഭക്ഷണം}} is the category they belong to — and a course can easily leave you able to order lunch and unable to say the word \emph{food}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bhakṣaṇaṁ}
  \item \emph{hōṭṭalil}
  \item \emph{bil}, then ask how many rupees
  \item which of the two borrowings would mislead somebody who trusted English
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do you find at a \emph{hōṭṭal}? (\textbf{Food}.) What is \emph{bhakṣaṇaṁ}? (\textbf{Food, the category}.) And what should you do with a borrowed word's original meaning? (\textbf{Check it rather than assume it}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
